motion: Islam is a religion of peace.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Imagine a community leader citing sacred authority to attack a peaceful minority. The victims experience that teaching as permission, not distortion. That concrete danger proves the motion is too broad and should be rejected.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Today's motion is, "Islam is a religion of peace." Rachel argues for it, and Russell argues against it. Each opening gets thirty seconds, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. Then each side gets a thirty-second closing, with a ten-second cue before time.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I support the motion because Islam teaches peace, mercy, and responsibility toward others. Violent acts by some followers do not define the faith itself, just as crimes by some citizens do not define every citizen. Its central moral direction is peaceful.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let him come back on that.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I oppose the motion because calling Islam a religion of peace overlooks teachings and traditions that have been used to justify violence. A label should reflect the whole record, not only its gentler passages. When a religion can authorize conflict against outsiders, the peaceful label becomes misleading.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Peaceful language exists, but its violent permissions still make the motion false.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds from this side?

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Now, on to round two. This is our middle round in which the debaters talk directly to one another. You have two and a half minutes, starting when I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I believe Islam always calls people toward peace. Its central teachings give believers a moral duty to protect life, restrain anger, and seek justice without turning faith into a license for violence.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Rachel, if Islam always calls people toward peace, how do you explain believers who sincerely use Islamic teachings to defend violence against civilians? Can a religion be peaceful when its own texts are invoked for that purpose?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: In the case of believers who sincerely use Islamic teachings to defend violence, Islam does not call people toward peace. That case shows how people can distort a faith while the motion still describes its moral core.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Rachel said i believe Islam always calls people toward peace, but islam does not call people toward peace.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: My first statement describes Islam's teaching, while my second describes what happens when believers misuse it. The religion's direction remains peaceful even when a follower rejects that direction and acts violently.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That misuse raises a wider policy question: should schools, courts, and public agencies treat religious claims as protected belief when those claims influence conduct? Equal rules need clear limits, especially when belief is used to excuse harm.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Please address the issue that I did raise, which is islam is a religion of peace.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The motion asks whether Islam is a religion of peace, and its violent permissions matter to that answer. A tradition that can be used to command violence cannot honestly be described as peaceful without ignoring part of what it teaches.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that violent interpretations deserve serious criticism, but Russell treats misuse as the faith's essence. That confuses a religion's principles with a follower's choice, and Islam's principles still direct believers toward peace, mercy, and human dignity when-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I interrupt because that distinction is the whole dispute. If the principles can support opposite commands, you cannot simply declare the peaceful reading authentic and dismiss the violent reading as misuse; the motion requires a fuller standard.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Russell says opposite interpretations make the peaceful description impossible. They do not: the existence of misuse does not erase a faith's dominant moral teaching, and Islam's call to mercy and restraint supports the motion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Rachel's weakest claim is that a dominant teaching settles the question. It does not. The motion says Islam is a religion of peace, not merely that peaceful teachings exist; permissions for violence make that broad claim unsound.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds left, both of you.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I reject the premise that any permission for violence cancels a religion's peaceful identity. Russell's standard would make every tradition defined-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. So now we move on to our closing round. Rachel, you have the floor first.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This motion turns on what defines a religion: its central moral teaching or every harmful act committed in its name. Islam's central teachings emphasize mercy, justice, restraint, and peace. Misuse by followers cannot overturn that identity, so the motion is true.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let Russell respond to it.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Rachel's best point is that Islam contains teachings about mercy and peace. I accept that those teachings exist, but they do not answer the whole question. A religion should not receive a peaceful label while its authority can also be used to justify violence. That contradiction matters because beliefs guide real choices. If the tradition permits competing readings, we must judge the danger as well as the ideal. The motion asks for a broad description, and broad descriptions must face the full record.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, now it's ten.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Islam may inspire peaceful conduct-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm sorry, you've hit time.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for taking part. This debate is now closed without declaring a winner.
